title: Detection Strategy for T1528 - Steal Application Access Token
shortTitle: Detection Strategy for T1528 - Steal Application Access T...
summary: This detection strategy covers theft of application access tokens, the technique tracked as T1528. Modern applications and command line tools hold bearer tokens and refresh tokens that grant access to mail, files, chat and cloud resources, and a stolen token can be used directly against the service from anywhere without a password prompt or a second factor challenge. The telemetry that makes it visible is identity provider token issuance and refresh records with the client identifier and source address, service side audit logs that show the same token used from a new address or a new client, endpoint file and memory access to token caches and command line credential files, and network records that place the token use outside the expected network. The strategy fails in practice because normal remote work, virtual private network changes and shared automation tokens produce the same impossible travel and unusual client patterns, so the rule needs a per application baseline of which client identifiers ever use which addresses.

beginner.definition: This rule looks for the theft of a digital pass that lets one application act for you. That pass is called an access token. You can think of it as a key card for a service rather than a key to your account. With a copy, an attacker can read your mail or files without logging in. The rule watches where a token is used and which address it comes from.
beginner.whyItMatters: Tokens are stored in memory, in browser storage and in small files on developer machines. They are easy to copy and easy to reuse. Use of a token often produces no failed sign in. So it does not look like an attack in the usual login reports. Revoking the token is the only reliable response, and that requires knowing which token was taken.
howItWorks: The identity provider records every time it issues or refreshes a token, with the client and the address.
The rule builds a picture of which applications normally use which addresses for each user.
A token used from an address that is new for that application is flagged for review.
Any use of a token by a client that never requested one before is treated as more serious.
The rule places the token use next to the user real location to find impossible travel.
The response step revokes the token and the refresh token, then asks the user to sign in again.
beginner.example: Imagine a hotel where your room key is a card. The card opens your door and the gym, and it carries no name. Anyone who picks up the card can use the gym and your room until the front desk cancels it. This rule watches for a card being used at two doors in two cities at once.
takeaways: An access token is a temporary key that works without the account password.
Failed sign in reports will not show token theft, so you need token use logs.
Revoke the refresh token too, or a new access token will simply be issued.

objectives: Explain what an application access token is and how it differs from a password.
Name the identity provider records that show token issue, refresh and use with source address.
Identify the endpoint files and memory regions where tokens are stored on workstations.
Build a baseline of expected client identifiers and addresses for each business application.
Recognise an impossible travel or hosting provider address as a token theft indicator.
Carry out a token revocation response that also invalidates the refresh token.
dataSources: Identity provider sign in and token issuance logs including client identifier, user, source address and application
Cloud service audit records for the mail, file and chat application programming interfaces that used the token
Endpoint file creation and file read events for command line tool credential directories and cached token files
Endpoint detection and response process command lines showing command line tool authentication activity
Proxy and firewall records that map the source address for an application programming interface call to a user session
logic: The pattern is a token that is used from an address or by a client application that has no precedent for that user and workload, especially when the same token or user appears from two locations that cannot both be current. The fields that must be correlated are the token or session identifier, the client application identifier, the user principal, the source address and the timestamp from the identity provider, joined to the application programming interface audit record that used that token. The malicious case usually shows a first use of a token by an unknown client, a source address hosted by a cloud provider rather than an internet service provider, and access to content the application never touched before. The benign case is a mobile device switching networks, a virtual private network exit changing, or a shared automation identity that legitimately runs from many addresses at once.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Application Access Token Used From New Address by Unknown Client
# logsource:
#   product: azure
# detection:
#   selection:
#     event_type: 'token issuance'
#     status: 'success'
#   filter_known:
#     client_app_id:
#       - 'approved mail client'
#       - 'approved automation agent'
#     network_zone: 'corporate'
#   condition: selection and not filter_known
# level: high
falsePositives: Staff who connect through a virtual private network whose exit address changes between sessions during the day
Automation and integration service identities that legitimately run from several addresses or hosting regions at once
Mobile devices that move between wireless networks and mobile data while a token is still valid
Security and reporting tools that replay a token to test application programming interface access in an authorised test
Developers who run a command line tool from a home network during an on call rotation
tuningNotes: Baseline for at least thirty days which client application identifiers and network ranges each identity uses, then alert only when both the client and the address are new, which removes most single factor noise. Add a filter for your known virtual private network and hosting ranges, and treat cloud provider address space as a scoring signal rather than an automatic alert. Keep the identity provider and application programming interface audit streams joined by token identifier, because that join is what separates token theft from a stolen password. The coverage you lose is a token reused from within an already trusted range or by an already known client.
